title: Native competitors reduced nitrogen-driven live biomass gains in two of three Arctic plants in a chamber experiment
abstract: We tested how much of the nitrogen-driven live biomass gain remained with native competitors after plants arrived. We used a separate factorial chamber experiment with three non-native Arctic plants, four native competitors, two soils and two temperatures. The analysis used 959 plants in 32 trays, included dead plants as zero live biomass, and resampled trays. Achillea retained 38% of its nitrogen gain with native competitors (three-species adjusted limits 11-71%). Barbarea retained 50% (23-82%). Deschampsia retained 59% (22-145%), so full retention remained possible. An exploratory paired-pot split assigned 70%, 50% and 42% of added biomass to native plants. Total paired-pot gains were positive. The source paper already reported stronger competition under added nitrogen. The new result is the response-retention estimate, mortality checks, tray uncertainty and paired-pot yield partition. This supports a limit on resource response after arrival, but does not measure nutrient uptake or a share of the thermal-tracking gap. Few chambers, endpoint labels, small pots and short duration limit inference. Code, aggregate evidence and exact external-data retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: Nitrogen-driven biomass gains retained with native competitors, and paired-pot gains. Panel A has intervals adjusted across three species. Panel B is exploratory and has ordinary 95% intervals.

citations.reason: Weak temporal tracking motivates a process test with independent experimental data.
Measured bird dispersal limitation motivates testing limits after arrival in a different system.
Original experiment and prior finding that native competition was stronger under added nitrogen. We quantify retained biomass response and allocation; we do not claim discovery of competition.
